cards.q: What kinds of beneficiary nomination are there?
cards.a: Super: binding (lapsing or non-lapsing) or non-binding. Flexi Pension also has reversionary (not for BIS). With no nomination, the Trustee decides.

sources.quote: Binding nomination (non-lapsing or lapsing), or

cards.q: Does a pension balance go to the member's estate automatically?
cards.a: No. Super and pensions don't automatically form part of the estate, so a nomination matters.

sources.quote: Your Flexi Pension account doesn't automatically form part of your estate

cards.q: What is a reversionary beneficiary?
cards.a: Someone whose income continues from the pension after the member dies, instead of a lump sum being paid. It overrides any other nomination on that pension.
cards.detail: Can't be split with other dependants. Not available for BIS. Can be nominated in the pension application or with the Reversionary beneficiary form.

sources.quote: A reversionary beneficiary nomination will override any other nomination you've made on your Flexi Pension account.
Income payments can't be split between your reversionary beneficiary and other dependants.

cards.q: Who can be a reversionary beneficiary?
cards.a: A spouse, a child, a financial dependant at death, or an interdependent (at nomination and at death). Children 18+ only if 18 to 24 and financially dependent, or disabled.
cards.detail: A child receives income until 25 (then a lump sum), unless disabled.

sources.quote: between age 18 and 24 and financially dependent on you immediately before your death, or
they'll continue to receive the income until age 25

cards.q: Can adding or removing a reversionary beneficiary affect Centrelink?
cards.a: It can, for example the assessable income for the income test. Suggest financial advice before changing it.

sources.quote: updating or removing a reversionary beneficiary may affect your assessable income payments for the income test.

cards.q: What's the difference between lapsing and non-lapsing binding nominations?
cards.a: Lapsing: expires three years after it was signed, last confirmed or amended. Non-lapsing: lasts until changed or revoked. A paper form with no choice ticked defaults to lapsing.

sources.quote: A valid binding death benefit nomination (lapsing) remains in effect for three years from the date it was first signed, last amended or confirmed.
If you don't make a choice when you complete your binding death benefit nomination paper form, your nomination will default to lapsing.

cards.q: How is a binding nomination made?
cards.a: Non-lapsing: online or on the paper form. Lapsing: paper form only, with two witnesses. It takes effect only once received and accepted.

sources.quote: Lapsing Binding death benefit nomination requests will need to be completed via the Binding death benefit nomination form
A binding death benefit nomination doesn't take effect until it has been received and accepted by the Trustee.

cards.q: What makes a binding nomination valid?
cards.a: Only dependants or the legal personal representative; 100% allocated exactly; paper forms signed and dated by the member (not a power of attorney) in front of two witnesses aged 18+ who aren't beneficiaries, with their declaration.

sources.quote: 100% of your benefit must be allocated (the entire nomination will be invalid if the allocation doesn't equal exactly 100%)
must be signed and dated by you (not a power of attorney) in the presence of two witnesses, both of whom are over the age of 18 and not nominated to receive the benefit

cards.q: What happens if a binding nomination is invalid or expires?
cards.a: It no longer binds the Trustee and is treated as non-binding.

sources.quote: If a nominated person is not a beneficiary at your date of death, or if your binding nomination is invalid, the Trustee will treat your nomination as a non-binding death benefit nomination.

cards.q: How is a lapsing nomination renewed?
cards.a: By a written notice signed and dated by the member before it expires. It's the member's responsibility.

sources.quote: You can do this by providing us with a written notice, signed and dated by you, to that effect.

cards.q: Does one binding nomination cover all of a member's accounts?
cards.a: It can: one nomination for all UniSuper accounts, or separate nominations for each.

sources.quote: or submit a single valid binding death benefit nomination to apply to all your UniSuper accounts

cards.q: Are there special binding nomination issues for DBD members?
cards.a: Yes, for DBD members who joined before 1 January 1990. See the Binding death benefit nomination fact sheet.

sources.quote: Binding death benefit nominations may have implications for DBD members who joined before 1 January 1990

cards.q: What is a non-binding nomination?
cards.a: A preference the Trustee considers but isn't bound by. It doesn't expire. Made or changed with the Change of details form.

sources.quote: A non-binding death benefit nomination will remain in place until it's amended or replaced, or until you make a valid binding death benefit nomination.
To make or update a non-binding death benefit nomination, you must complete the Change of details form available at unisuper.com.au/forms.

cards.q: What happens with no nomination?
cards.a: The Trustee pays dependants and/or the legal personal representative in proportions it decides. With neither, it pays whoever superannuation law allows.

sources.quote: If you haven't nominated any beneficiaries, when you die the Trustee must pay the remaining balance of your Flexi Pension (if any) to one or more of your dependants and/or legal personal representatives in proportions determined by the Trustee.

cards.q: Who counts as a dependant for super?
aliases: can i leave my super to my kids
cards.a: A spouse (including de facto, any sex), children of any age, an interdependent at death, and anyone the Trustee considers was financially dependent at death.

sources.quote: your children (regardless of age)

cards.q: Who counts as a dependant for tax on a death benefit?
cards.a: A spouse or former spouse, children under 18, an interdependent, or a financial dependant at the date of death. {{adult-children-tax:{{adult-children-tax:Adult children are usually not tax dependants.}}}}

sources.quote: your child(ren) under the age of 18

cards.q: What is an interdependency relationship?
cards.a: Two people living together in a close relationship where one or both provide financial and domestic support and care. A statutory declaration is needed before payment, on the Applying for a death benefit form.

sources.quote: Before any benefit can be paid to a person with whom you had an interdependency relationship, the Trustee requires a statutory declaration

cards.q: What is the legal personal representative?
cards.a: The executor of the will, or the estate administrator. A benefit paid to them becomes part of the estate.

sources.quote: Your legal personal representative is the executor of your Will or the administrator of your estate if you die without a Will.

cards.q: How are lump sum death benefits taxed?
cards.a: Tax-free to a tax dependant. To a non-dependant: up to 17% on the taxed element and 32% on any untaxed element; the tax-free component is untaxed.

sources.quote: up to 17% tax is withheld on any taxed element, and 32% on any untaxed element

cards.q: How is a death benefit pension taxed?
cards.a: Tax-free if the deceased was 60+ at death or the beneficiary is 60+ (and a tax dependant). If both are under 60, the taxable component is taxed at marginal rates with a 15% offset.

sources.quote: If the deceased was aged 60 or over at the date of death, and/or the beneficiary is age 60 or over when receiving the retirement income payments
